raw_statement: By 31 December 2031, unaffordability is absorbed through changed housing formats rather than restored ownership: the US first-time-buyer share of home purchases stays below its 2015–2019 average, median new-home size continues to fall, multigenerational households exceed 20% of US households, and manufactured/modular units plus build-to-rent take a materially larger share of new supply than in 2025.
title: Format Absorption: How Housing Unaffordability Is Resolved by Changing the Product, Not the Price

formalized.statement: [Hypothesis] By 31 December 2031, US housing unaffordability is absorbed primarily through format substitution rather than restored ownership access. Operationally: (A) the NAR first-time-buyer share of existing-home purchases in the 2031 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers remains below the 2015-2019 average (~32-33%); (B) median new single-family completion size (Census Characteristics of New Housing) in 2031 is below the 2025 level and >12% below the 2015 peak of ~2,467 sq ft; (C) the share of US households containing two or more adult generations (Pew/IPUMS-CPS definition) exceeds 20%; (D) combined manufactured/modular shipments plus dedicated build-to-rent single-family completions exceed 2025's share of total new housing units delivered by at least 3 percentage points. The thesis resolves TRUE if at least three of four conditions hold at year-end 2031.
formalized.population: US households forming or re-forming between 2026 and 2031 (renters aged 25-44, adult children living with parents, downsizing 65+ owners) plus the homebuilding, manufactured-housing and institutional rental supply chain serving them.
formalized.behavior: Households adapt to a ~5% risk-free rate, 7%+ mortgages and a frozen resale market by changing the format of shelter consumed - smaller units, longer tenure, renting a detached house instead of owning one, sharing a roof across generations, buying a factory-built unit - instead of waiting for affordability to be restored by lower rates or falling prices.
formalized.observable_outcome: A composite of four independently published series moving in the same direction: depressed first-time-buyer share, shrinking median new-home size, rising multigenerational household share, and rising manufactured/modular + build-to-rent share of new supply.
formalized.measurable_metric: Four-condition composite (3-of-4 threshold): (A) NAR first-time-buyer share <32%; (B) Census median new SF home size <2,170 sq ft and below 2025 print; (C) Pew/IPUMS multigenerational household share >20%; (D) (manufactured shipments + modular + BTR SF completions) / total new housing units delivered, up >=3pp vs 2025 baseline (~13-15% [estimate, definition-sensitive]).

mechanism.human_motivation: [Inference] Shelter demand is a need, not a preference; when the price of the standard format (30-year-financed detached ownership) exceeds what income and credit permit, households do not exit the market - they re-specify the product. Secondary motivations: preserving optionality on location and job mobility, pooling household balance sheets under inflation, and avoiding a purchase that locks in a 7-8% coupon that feels like a mistake if rates fall.
mechanism.friction_removed: [Observation/Inference] The frictions being removed are not technological but legal and financial: ADU and missing-middle zoning liberalization (CA, WA, MT, OR), HUD code modernization and CrossMod/FHA Title I reform enabling factory-built homes to be mortgaged as real property, and institutional capital making single-family renting a service you can buy at scale rather than a landlord relationship you must negotiate. Also removed: the social friction on adult children living at home and on renting a house long-term.
mechanism.enabling_technology: [Observation] Factory-built and volumetric modular production, panelized framing and CNC-cut kits, construction robotics; property-management software and institutional underwriting that make 100,000 scattered rental houses operable as one asset; iBuyer/listing data infrastructure that prices rental-vs-own arbitrage. [Assumption] None of these are frontier technologies - the binding inputs are financing and land-use law, not engineering.
mechanism.economic_incentive: [Inference] With ~5% risk-free and 7%+ mortgages, the user cost of owning exceeds rent in nearly every major US metro; capital earns more renting the house than selling it, builders earn more delivering smaller units and BTR communities to institutional buyers than fighting for a shrinking mortgage-qualified buyer pool, and households save hundreds of dollars monthly per square foot forgone. Homebuilder incentive/buydown spend is already a de facto price cut delivered as format subsidy.
mechanism.trust_requirement: [Inference] Three trust conditions: (1) renters must trust institutional landlords enough to accept permanent tenancy (regulatory and reputational risk); (2) lenders, appraisers and buyers must trust factory-built homes to hold value like site-built (historically the Achilles heel); (3) families must trust intra-household arrangements that pool money across generations. Trust deficits, not economics, killed prior manufactured-housing cycles.
mechanism.distribution_mechanism: Production builders (LEN, DHI, PHM) shifting mix to smaller plans and BTR takeouts; manufactured-housing retail and community channels (CVCO, SKY, Clayton/BRK, ELS, SUI); institutional SFR platforms (INVH, AMH, TCN) and BTR developers; local government via zoning reform and ADU permitting; renovation/repair channel (HD, LOW, SHW, FND) serving repair-and-stay-put and multigenerational retrofits.
mechanism.network_effects: [Inference] Weak-to-moderate and mostly local: BTR and manufactured-home communities gain density economies within metros; appraisal comparables improve as factory-built stock accumulates (a genuine reflexive loop); social normalization of renting and multigenerational living is a fashion/diffusion effect rather than a true network effect. No winner-take-all dynamic.
mechanism.switching_costs: [Inference] Asymmetric and mostly one-way: once a household rents a detached house or moves in with parents, re-entry into ownership requires simultaneous down-payment accumulation and a rate/price reversal. On the supply side, factory capacity is high fixed cost - builders switch mix slowly and abandon it fast in downturns (Katerra lesson). Existing owners with sub-4% mortgages face enormous switching costs to move, which is itself the source of the frozen resale market.
mechanism.regulatory_constraints: [Observation] The dominant variable. Zoning and minimum lot sizes, HUD-code preemption fights, chattel-lending rules (manufactured homes financed as personal property at 8-11%), GSE duty-to-serve execution, state and local anti-institutional-landlord bills, rent control expansion, impact fees, and tariffs on lumber/appliances. [Inference] Policy can either accelerate the thesis (ADU/missing-middle reform, Title I expansion) or blunt one leg of it (BTR ownership restrictions), but it is very unlikely to restore the pre-2020 first-time-buyer channel by 2031.

analogues.name: Levittown and postwar industrialized tract housing
analogues.mechanism: Unmet shelter demand at unaffordable prices resolved by radically standardizing and shrinking the product (750-1,100 sq ft), plus federal credit - format substitution on the supply side.
analogues.lesson: Format substitution scales fast when cheap standardized supply and a government-backed financing channel arrive together; absent the credit leg, the format alone does not clear.

analogues.name: US manufactured housing boom (and credit-driven bust)
analogues.mechanism: Factory-built units absorbed low- and middle-income shelter demand, reaching ~30% of new single-family units sold in peak years, then collapsed when chattel securitization failed.
analogues.lesson: The single most direct precedent: factory-built share is a financing variable, not a manufacturing variable. Watch chattel spreads and FHA Title I, not factory capacity.

analogues.name: 1970s stagflation: condo conversion and mobile-home surge
analogues.mechanism: Double-digit mortgage rates froze the standard format; demand rerouted into condos, mobile homes, creative financing and doubling-up rather than waiting for rates to fall.
analogues.lesson: Closest macro analogue. Households adapted within ~5-7 years; when rates finally fell after 1982 the adaptations partially reversed - format shifts are sticky but not permanent if the rate shock reverses hard.

analogues.name: Japan post-bubble: rental permanence and compact urban units
analogues.mechanism: Permanent repricing of shelter capital led to smaller units, longer tenure, later household formation and normalized lifetime renting.
analogues.lesson: When the wealth-building rationale for ownership dies, size and tenure adjust for decades. Also a warning: adaptation coincided with collapsing household formation, not just format change.

analogues.name: Japanese prefab housing industry (Sekisui House, Daiwa)
analogues.mechanism: Industrialized housing captured ~15% of new detached homes by pairing factory production with bank-grade financing and brand warranty.
analogues.lesson: Factory housing wins share only where lenders and buyers treat the product as equivalent collateral; brand and warranty solved the trust problem that US chattel lending never did.

analogues.name: Nordic modular/panelized construction dominance
analogues.mechanism: Centralized land-use policy and cold-climate build-season constraints pushed most detached housing into factories.
analogues.lesson: Industrialized supply share is set by land-use centralization; the fragmented US permitting landscape is the main reason to discount the fastest modular scenarios.

analogues.name: UK 'Generation Rent' plus shared ownership
analogues.mechanism: Post-GFC credit tightening permanently lowered the first-time-buyer share; demand absorbed by private rented sector, shared-ownership hybrids and parental co-financing.
analogues.lesson: First-time-buyer share can stay depressed for a full decade despite continuous political intervention; the intergenerational transfer channel ('Bank of Mum and Dad') becomes the real qualifying mechanism.

analogues.name: Germany/Switzerland persistent rental-majority equilibrium
analogues.mechanism: Tenant-protective law plus institutional rental supply makes lifetime renting a stable, high-status format rather than a failure state.
analogues.lesson: Rental permanence is a viable steady state, but it requires tenant-security law the US mostly lacks - without it, US format absorption is more fragile and more politically contested.

analogues.name: Hong Kong / Tokyo 'nano-flat' micro-unit normalization
analogues.mechanism: Extreme land cost absorbed by shrinking the unit to the minimum socially tolerable size rather than by price decline.
analogues.lesson: Unit-size shrinkage is the fastest-acting absorption channel and has no obvious floor until regulation imposes one.

analogues.name: Rise of US multigenerational households
analogues.mechanism: Economic pressure plus immigration composition drove the share of Americans in multigenerational households from ~12% to ~18%, reversing a century-long decline.
analogues.lesson: The trend is real and monotonic but SLOW (~0.15pp/yr). Getting from ~18% to >20% by 2031 requires acceleration, not continuation - this is the weakest leg of the four-condition composite.

analogues.name: Post-GFC institutional single-family rental (Invitation Homes, AMH)
analogues.mechanism: Capital bought the housing stock households could no longer finance and sold it back as a service - control traded for access.
analogues.lesson: Institutionalizing a formerly owner-occupied asset class took under a decade and survived a political backlash; the model needed a distressed entry price, which the 2026 market does not offer - hence BTR (new build) replaces buy-to-rent.

analogues.name: US build-to-rent single-family emergence
analogues.mechanism: Builders bypassed the mortgage-qualified buyer entirely by selling communities to institutional owners.
analogues.lesson: Already ~9-10% of single-family starts from near zero in seven years [estimate]. The in-progress leg of the thesis; the risk is that BTR is itself rate-sensitive and cap-rate-constrained at 5% risk-free.

analogues.name: California ADU legalization
analogues.mechanism: Legal friction removal converted latent backyard capacity into tens of thousands of units per year - informal density as an affordability release valve.
analogues.lesson: When the constraint is legal rather than economic, removing it produces a step-change in ~5 years; ADUs are also the physical substrate of multigenerational living, linking conditions (C) and (D).

analogues.name: Auto affordability absorbed via leasing and 72-84 month terms
analogues.mechanism: Rather than buy cheaper cars, households extended terms, leased, or bought used - format/tenure substitution to preserve the consumption level.
analogues.lesson: Consumers reliably re-specify the financing and tenure of a big-ticket durable rather than abandon it; expect analogous mortgage-term and shared-equity innovations in housing.

analogues.name: Music/film ownership displaced by subscription streaming
analogues.mechanism: Access replaced ownership once the access format was cheaper and more convenient; prior 'ownership' norms collapsed within a decade.
analogues.lesson: Access-over-ownership transitions complete fast when access is BETTER, not just cheaper - housing rental is cheaper but not better, so expect slower, grudging adoption and reversal risk.

analogues.name: Enterprise capex-to-opex shift to cloud
analogues.mechanism: Owning the asset was replaced by renting capacity from a professional operator; control traded for flexibility and lower entry cost.
analogues.lesson: Professionalized landlords of a previously owner-operated asset base capture durable margin; the analogue supports institutional rental operators as the value pool, not the tenants.

analogues.name: Airline seat-pitch shrinkage and basic-economy unbundling
analogues.mechanism: Cost pressure absorbed by silently shrinking the product and unbundling amenities while holding the headline price.
analogues.lesson: Product shrinkage meets remarkably little consumer resistance when the alternative is not consuming at all; median new-home size decline is the housing version and has no natural stopping point.

analogues.name: Grocery shrinkflation and private-label trade-down
analogues.mechanism: Inflation absorbed by package size and brand substitution rather than demand destruction.
analogues.lesson: Format absorption is the default consumer response to unaffordability and shows up in official statistics within 2-3 years - the fast-acting confirmation that quantity, not price, is the adjusting variable.

analogues.name: US tiny-house and micro-unit movement
analogues.mechanism: Attempted radical downsizing as an affordability solution; blocked by zoning minimums, financing gaps and buyer resale fear.
analogues.lesson: The clearest failure case: enthusiasm and economics were not enough against minimum-lot-size rules and mortgage ineligibility. Format shifts that require BOTH new law and new financing usually stall.

analogues.name: Katerra and the venture-funded modular construction wave
analogues.mechanism: Attempted to industrialize housing supply with fixed-cost factories against cyclical, geographically fragmented demand; ended in bankruptcy.
analogues.lesson: The supply-side leg (condition D) has a high historical failure rate in the US. Incumbent HUD-code manufacturers with dealer networks and community land (CVCO, SKY, Clayton) are far likelier winners than de novo modular platforms.

analogues.name: Co-living operators (WeLive, Common, Starcity)
analogues.mechanism: Attempted to monetize shared-roof living as a branded product for unrelated adults.
analogues.lesson: Sharing a roof scales through FAMILY, not through branded operators - supports the multigenerational leg of the thesis while discrediting the commercialized co-living version of it.

reference_class.description: Transitions in which a durable, need-driven good becomes unaffordable at prevailing income and credit terms, and demand is cleared by FORMAT SUBSTITUTION - smaller units, longer tenure, shared consumption, access-instead-of-ownership, or industrialized/standardized supply - rather than by price reversion or restored credit access. The class spans housing (postwar tract, 1970s mobile homes/condos, post-bubble Japan, UK Generation Rent, HK nano-flats, ADUs, BTR, SFR), and non-housing durables where the same mechanism operates (autos via leasing/term extension, media via streaming, IT via cloud, airlines and groceries via shrinkage). Base-rate observation: the DEMAND-side legs (smaller product, longer tenure, shared households, renting instead of owning) occurred in roughly 16 of 19 cases, typically visible in official statistics within 3-10 years of the price shock. The SUPPLY-side industrialization leg (factory-built share gains) succeeded in about half of cases and only where financing treated the factory product as equivalent collateral and land-use rules permitted it; where either condition failed (US tiny homes, Katerra), it failed outright. Composite implication: conditions (A) first-time-buyer share, (B) home size, and (D) BTR/manufactured share sit in the high-base-rate demand-and-capital-routing subclass, while condition (C) multigenerational share sits in a slow-moving demographic subclass with a historical drift of only ~0.1-0.2pp per year.
reference_class.caveats: [Measurement] Condition C is definition-sensitive: Census 'multigenerational' (3+ generations) is ~6% of households while the Pew/IPUMS two-adult-generation definition is ~18% of the population - the thesis must be scored against a pre-specified series or it is unfalsifiable, and the 20% threshold may already be near-met or far-off depending on the choice. [Measurement] NAR's first-time-buyer series is a small, response-biased survey with known level shifts; direction is more reliable than level. [Confounding] A rate collapse to sub-5% mortgages before 2029 would partially reverse conditions A and B (1982-86 precedent) though format shifts are sticky and would not fully unwind by 2031. [Selection] Analogue set over-samples completed transitions with published data; failed format shifts are under-recorded, likely biasing the base rate upward by an unknown amount. [Independence] Conditions A, B and D are not independent - all four are driven by the same cost-of-capital shock, so a 3-of-4 composite is far less demanding than four independent coin flips; conversely a single macro reversal moves three of them together. [Policy] Anti-institutional-landlord legislation, tariffs on building inputs, and GSE/Title I reform are discrete, hard-to-forecast jumps that could invert condition D specifically without touching A-C. [Horizon] Five years is short for supply-chain industrialization (historical analogues took 15-20 years) and long for demand-side adaptation (3-10 years) - expect the thesis to resolve mostly on the demand legs.

evidence.claim: NAR Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers shows the first-time-buyer share at a record-low 24% (2024) and ~21% in the 2025 edition, with median first-time-buyer age rising to 38-40 — already far below the 2015-2019 average of ~32-33%.
evidence.source: NAR Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers 2024/2025

evidence.claim: Census Characteristics of New Housing shows median size of completed single-family homes falling from the ~2,467 sq ft 2015 peak to roughly 2,150-2,200 sq ft in 2024-2025, as production builders re-mixed toward entry-level plans and smaller lots.
evidence.source: US Census Bureau, Characteristics of New Housing; NAHB builder mix commentary

evidence.claim: 30-year fixed mortgage rate at 7.45% (20-month high) with credible 8% talk, 30-year Treasury at post-2004 highs and the Fed signalling further hikes — user cost of owning exceeds market rent in nearly every large US metro, making format substitution the only available adjustment margin for new households.

Rate lock-in persists: a large majority of outstanding US mortgages carry sub-5% coupons, keeping existing-home turnover near multi-decade lows and starving the first-time-buyer channel of entry-level resale inventory regardless of demand.
evidence.source: FHFA/ICE mortgage monitor; NAR existing-home sales series

evidence.claim: Dedicated single-family build-to-rent completions hit successive records (~30-40k/yr in 2023-2024 with a ~100k pipeline), reaching roughly 10% of single-family starts in some quarters — institutional capital is now a structural takeout channel for builders.
evidence.source: John Burns Research / NAHB / Yardi Matrix BTR trackers

evidence.claim: Manufactured-housing shipments rose to ~103k units in 2024 (best since 2006) and continued growing in 2025, aided by GSE duty-to-serve, FHA Title I modernization and CrossMod products that let factory-built homes be financed as real property.
evidence.source: MHI/Census manufactured housing survey; FHFA duty-to-serve filings

evidence.claim: ADU legalization has moved from experiment to material supply: ADUs account for a high-teens-to-~20% share of new housing permits in California's largest cities, with WA, OR, MT and several metros following — the legal friction, not the construction technology, was the binding constraint and it is being removed.
evidence.source: CA HCD permit data; Terner Center; state missing-middle statutes

evidence.claim: Builders are delivering de facto price cuts as format subsidies — incentives and rate buydowns running ~8-13% of price, alongside guidance cuts (Lennar) and one-year-low builder confidence — which economically favors shrinking the product and selling to rental aggregators over chasing a shrinking mortgage-qualified buyer pool.

Consumer behavior is already adapting through repair-and-stay-put and household pooling rather than transacting — a pattern visible in home-improvement/MRO demand resilience against collapsing turnover, with LOW, HD, SHW and LEN flagged as not priced for it.

The multigenerational leg is definition-fragile: Pew's widely cited 18% figure is the share of the US *population* living in multigenerational households (59.7M), while the share of *households* under the two-adult-generation definition is meaningfully lower (~13-17%). Crossing 20% of households by 2031 requires an acceleration, not a continuation, of the existing trend.

A genuine price correction restores, rather than suppresses, first-time-buyer share: after 2008 the NAR FTB share jumped to 47-50%, and current conditions (58% seller surplus, 'the housing slide could become a crash' commentary, builder discounting) point toward exactly that corrective channel over a six-year horizon.

Six years is long enough for the rate regime to reverse: if the current hiking cycle ends in 2027 and mortgages normalize toward 5-5.5% by 2029-2031, the largest-ever 30-40 year old cohort plus accumulated pent-up demand could push FTB share back above 32% and reverse the median-size decline as mix shifts up.
evidence.source: Demographic cohort projections; rate-path scenario analysis

evidence.claim: Modular/volumetric construction has repeatedly failed to scale in the US — Katerra's ~$2bn collapse, Veev's insolvency, and modular's persistent sub-5% share of completions for four decades — because factory fixed cost plus fragmented local codes and appraisal comps defeat the unit-economics argument in every downcycle.
evidence.source: Industry post-mortems; Census/MBI modular share data

evidence.claim: Political backlash against institutional single-family ownership is escalating (federal 'End Hedge Fund Control of American Homes' proposals, state-level acquisition limits and transfer-tax surcharges), which can cap the build-to-rent leg even while the underlying demand persists.
evidence.source: State legislative trackers; congressional bill filings

evidence.claim: Manufactured-home financing remains mostly chattel at 8-11% with short amortization and weak appraisal comparables; without a durable conversion to real-property mortgages, factory-built share is rate-elastic and gives back gains quickly when consumer credit tightens.
evidence.source: CFPB manufactured housing finance reports; MHI

evidence.claim: Higher-for-longer rates are simultaneously a headwind to the *supply* side of the thesis: institutional SFR/BTR takeouts, manufactured-home community roll-ups and modular factories are all levered, cap-rate-sensitive businesses whose cost of capital has risen as much as the homebuyer's, slowing delivery of the very formats households are substituting into.

prerequisites_met: Price signal is unambiguous and persistent: 7%+ mortgages, ~5% risk-free, user cost above rent in nearly every metro
Legal friction removal underway: ADU/missing-middle statutes in CA/WA/OR/MT, HUD-code modernization, FHA Title I reform, GSE duty-to-serve
Social normalization: renting a detached house long-term and adult children at home carry little stigma; NAR FTB share at record lows for three consecutive surveys
Supply-side channel exists at scale: production builders now sell communities wholesale to BTR aggregators; manufactured shipments at 19-year highs
Operating infrastructure for scattered-site rental (property management software, underwriting, maintenance networks) proven across a full decade post-GFC
prerequisites_missing: Mortgage-eligible financing for factory-built homes at scale — chattel lending at 8-11% still dominates
Appraisal comparables and resale liquidity for modular/CrossMod stock (the reflexive loop is early)
Political durability of institutional single-family rental under an anti-landlord legislative cycle
Multigenerational household share crossing the 20% *household* threshold, which requires acceleration beyond the current trend
Zoning liberalization outside a handful of states; most metros still enforce minimum lot sizes that block small-format delivery
stage.historical_pathway_position: Roughly where auto affordability stood around 1998-2002 (leasing and term-extension absorbing price, ownership economics quietly abandoned) and where US enterprise IT stood around 2011-2013 in the capex-to-opex shift: the behavioral substitution is already mass-market and visible in the headline statistics, but the institutional plumbing (financing, appraisal, regulation) that makes it permanent rather than cyclical is only half-built. Crossing-the-chasm is done for renting-permanence and size shrinkage; the factory-built and BTR legs are still early adopters.

bull.description: Rates stay structurally high (mortgages 6.5-8% through 2029), no price crash large enough to restore entry-level affordability, and policy actively subsidizes format substitution: Title I/CrossMod financing converts a meaningful slice of manufactured homes to real-property mortgages, ADU and missing-middle reform spreads to 15+ states, BTR survives the legislative backlash with disclosure rather than ownership caps. All four conditions resolve TRUE — FTB share under 26%, median new size under 2,100 sq ft, multigenerational household share over 20% on the IPUMS definition, factory-built plus BTR up 4-6pp of new supply. Shelter is definitively re-priced as a consumed service; the repair/MRO, factory-built and rental-operations complexes gain durable pricing power.

base.description: Three of four conditions hold, with the multigenerational leg the most likely to miss on definitional grounds. FTB share stays in the 21-28% range — depressed but partially recovering if 2028-2030 brings mortgage rates near 6%; median new-home size continues grinding down toward ~2,050-2,150 sq ft as builders keep the entry-level mix; manufactured shipments plus BTR add 3-5pp of new supply, concentrated in Sun Belt metros. The thesis resolves TRUE but as a slow grind rather than a regime break, and the equity payoff accrues to the boring channel (building products, repair, land, trades) rather than to any disruptive format platform.

bear.description: The cost-of-capital shock resolves through prices and policy rather than formats: a 15-25% national correction in real terms plus a 2027-2029 easing cycle restores entry-level affordability, FTB share rebounds above 32% as it did in 2009-2012, mix normalizes and median new-home size stabilizes or ticks up. Simultaneously, anti-institutional-landlord legislation caps BTR growth and a consumer-credit contraction crushes chattel-financed manufactured-home sales, so the supply-format leg stalls. Fewer than three conditions hold; the 'format substitution' behavior turns out to have been a cyclical rationing response, not a structural re-specification of shelter.

supporting: NAR Profile first-time-buyer share printing below 26% in the 2026 and 2027 editions
Census median size of completed single-family homes printing below 2,150 sq ft for two consecutive years
Manufactured-housing shipments sustaining above 110k units with a rising share financed as real property (GSE duty-to-serve loan counts)
BTR share of single-family starts holding above 10% through a builder downcycle rather than collapsing with cap rates
Builder earnings calls explicitly guiding to smaller average square footage and higher BTR/community-sale mix
ADU permits exceeding 10% of new units in three or more additional states
Home-improvement comps holding up while existing-home turnover falls (repair-and-stay-put signature)
IPUMS-CPS household-level multigenerational share crossing 17-18% on the way to 20%
contradictory: 30-year mortgage back under 6% with purchase applications up >25% y/y
NAR FTB share rebounding above 30% in any single survey year
Median new-home size rising two years running as builders re-mix upward
State or federal legislation materially restricting institutional single-family ownership or imposing rent control across Sun Belt BTR markets
Manufactured-housing shipments falling below 90k on consumer-credit tightening
A named modular/factory-built scale-up failing publicly (Katerra rerun), freezing capital into the channel
Existing-home inventory surging as sub-4% mortgage holders capitulate, restoring the starter-home resale channel
indicators.next_confirmation_signal: The November 2026 NAR Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers (first-time-buyer share and median FTB age) read alongside the Census 2026 Characteristics of New Housing median completed size — two independently produced series landing within weeks of each other. A third consecutive sub-26% FTB print combined with a sub-2,150 sq ft median size would confirm two of four legs six years early.
biggest_variables: The 2027-2029 rate path — whether ~5% risk-free is regime or anomaly is the single largest determinant of the FTB leg
Whether a price correction happens and how deep (a crash resolves affordability through prices and falsifies the thesis)
Political treatment of institutional single-family rental at state and federal level
Execution of manufactured-home financing reform (chattel-to-mortgage conversion), which determines whether factory-built is a cycle or a channel
Speed and breadth of zoning/ADU liberalization outside the current four or five reform states
Definitional resolution of the multigenerational metric (population share vs household share) — the weakest of the four legs

value_pools.layer: Repair, renovation and MRO (repair-and-stay-put, multigenerational retrofit, ADU conversion)
value_pools.emerging_need: Households that cannot move instead spend on the house they have: in-law suites, basement conversions, second kitchens, ADUs, deferred-maintenance catch-up on an aging stock
value_pools.opportunity: Renovation spend decouples from transaction volume for the first time in modern cycles; ticket sizes shrink but frequency and repeat rate rise, and professional-contractor mix improves margin

value_pools.emerging_need: Deliver a smaller, cheaper, faster unit and sell it wholesale to rental aggregators when the mortgage-qualified buyer pool shrinks
value_pools.opportunity: Builders with land banked at entry-level price points and the balance sheet to survive incentive-funded margin compression consolidate share; community-scale sales to BTR buyers become a countercyclical order book

value_pools.layer: Entitled, serviced land near employment — and skilled trades
value_pools.emerging_need: Small-format delivery still requires lots, permits, water, power hookups and electricians/plumbers; factory production does not remove site work
value_pools.opportunity: The genuinely non-substitutable input. Trades labor and entitled lots capture the margin that leaves the finished-house price

value_pools.emerging_need: Demand for 3,000+ sq ft on large lots shrinks structurally as formation-stage households opt out and boomers eventually release inventory
value_pools.opportunity: Square footage itself becomes the commodity; premium migrates to location, energy cost and maintenance burden rather than size

value_pools.layer: Rental operations infrastructure (property management software, maintenance networks, underwriting, insurance)
value_pools.emerging_need: Permanent tenancy at scale requires operating 100,000 scattered detached houses as a single asset with trust-grade service levels
value_pools.opportunity: The toll road on format substitution: the operator layer earns whether the underlying asset appreciates or not; insurance pricing power on rental-occupied detached stock

value_pools.layer: Consumer credit and transaction finance tied to mortgage origination
value_pools.emerging_need: Household formation increasingly happens without a mortgage being created — the credit-creation event disappears from the economy
value_pools.opportunity: Inverse: purchase-mortgage volume, title, escrow, brokerage commission and move-driven big-ticket credit shrink as a share of household spend; the remaining credit demand shifts to chattel, rent-reporting and small-ticket renovation lending

value_pools.layer: Smaller-unit consumption bundle (value retail, compact goods, storage, delivery density)
value_pools.emerging_need: Less square footage per household means fewer and smaller durables, more off-site storage, more frequent small-basket and delivered purchases
value_pools.opportunity: Trade-down and unit-count retailers benefit while big-ticket furnishing and large-appliance volumes fall; delivery density improves in BTR communities

value_pools.layer: Political and regulatory exposure of institutional landlords

second_order_thesis: [Inference] The non-obvious consequence is monetary, not architectural. If household formation stops requiring a mortgage, the primary channel through which US monetary policy transmits to the real economy atrophies: shelter demand is satisfied by corporate balance sheets (BTR aggregators, manufactured-housing communities, parents' existing equity) rather than by household credit creation. That has three follow-ons. First, rate cuts become less stimulative than the Fed expects, because the marginal shelter consumer no longer levers up when rates fall — which argues for a structurally higher policy rate to achieve the same cooling, reinforcing the very condition that caused the substitution (a reflexive loop, not a cycle). Second, CPI shelter becomes stickier and more rent-weighted: converting would-be owners into permanent renters mechanically raises rent demand while the owner-equivalent component dampens, keeping measured inflation above target longer and validating the 65-months-above-2% regime in the briefs. Third, the economic value of housing migrates from the price of the asset to the cash flow of operating it — which is a transfer of pricing power from homeowners and mortgage originators to operators, maintenance/MRO supply chains, trades labor and entitled land. The investable expression is therefore not the disruptive format itself (modular has failed four times and BTR carries political risk) but the boring, non-substitutable inputs every format still consumes: lots, electricians, paint, lumber packages, HVAC, property-management and insurance. [Inference] The market is currently pricing housing as a rate derivative; the thesis says it should be priced as a consumption-and-services annuity, which is why LOW, HD, SHW and LEN show up in the not-priced bucket at the same moment builder confidence hits a one-year low.
losers: Toll Brothers and the large-format move-up builders — square footage is the commodity being shed
Purchase-mortgage origination, title, escrow and brokerage commission pools — household formation without a credit-creation event
Existing homeowners counting on move-up equity extraction; the sub-4% mortgage is an asset that cannot be sold without destroying it
Furniture, large-appliance and big-ticket durable manufacturers levered to turnover and square footage
Suburban large-lot land banks and municipalities whose fiscal model depends on detached-ownership transfer taxes and impact fees
Venture-funded modular platforms attempting to disintermediate the site-built supply chain — the Katerra failure mode recurs in every downcycle
Levered single-asset and small-scale landlords competing against institutional operating scale and facing the same rent-control backlash without the lobbying capacity
Home-equity-dependent consumer credit franchises and REIT roll-ups whose moat was cheap capital (AXP-style affluent-homeowner spend, net-lease and retail REITs priced against a 5.4% long bond)
Cities and states that do not liberalize zoning — they export their household formation to metros that do, losing the tax base rather than the demand

source_bullets.text: Housing preference adapts to unaffordability rather than resolving it \u2014 prefab/export home factories pivoting, builders cutting price rather than building more. Expect demand to migrate to smaller, manufactured and rented formats, permanently reducing the size of the first-time-buyer cohort.

Housing demand is structurally unmet regardless of rates (Buffett buying 10% of Lennar the day after a guidance cut), so the behavioural adaptation is smaller units, longer tenure, multigenerational households and rental permanence rather than ownership.
